title: Parashurama and the Retreating Sea
text: Long ago the sage Parashurama stood on the western hills and wished for new land where people could live. He hurled his axe far out over the water. Where it fell, the sea drew back, and a long green strip of coast appeared: the Konkan and the Malabar. Fishers say the sea still remembers, and that it comes close in the monsoon as if asking for its land back.
lesson: Coasts are shared with the sea, so respect its moods.

title: Matsya and the Great Flood
text: A tiny fish begged the king Manu to save it from bigger fish. Manu kept it in a jar, then a pond, then a river, and each time it grew. At last the fish became huge and revealed itself as the god Vishnu. It warned Manu that a great flood was coming and told him to build a boat. When the waters rose, the fish towed the boat to safety, carrying the seeds of life for a new beginning.
lesson: Kindness to the smallest creature can save the world.

title: The Drowned City of Dwarka
text: Tradition says Krishna built the shining city of Dwarka beside the western sea. After he left the world, the sea rose and covered the city. Divers and marine archaeologists have studied underwater stone structures off Dwarka and Bet Dwarka, though scholars still debate how old they are. Gujarat's fishers grew up on this tale: today's shore may be tomorrow's sea.
lesson: Coastlines change. The sea is powerful, so stay humble before it.

title: Poompuhar, the Port the Sea Took
text: Poompuhar, also called Kaveripoompattinam, was a busy port where the river Kaveri meets the sea. Tamil epics such as Silappatikaram and Manimekalai sing of its ships, markets and seaside festivals. Manimekalai also tells that the sea swallowed the city, and that a sea goddess watched over travellers on the waves. Underwater surveys have searched the sea floor near Poompuhar for traces of the old port.
lesson: Great ports can vanish. Memory is how a coast survives.

title: Bonbibi, Lady of the Forest
text: In the mangrove forests of the Sundarbans, honey-gatherers, woodcutters and fishers pray to Bonbibi, lady of the forest. The tale says a greedy tiger-spirit, Dakshin Rai, wanted to eat a poor boy named Dukhe. The boy called on Bonbibi, and she saved him. Her rule for everyone who enters the forest is simple: take only what you need, and never be greedy. People of different faiths honour her together.
lesson: Take only what you need. Greed brings danger.

title: Kalijai of Chilika
text: On a small island in Chilika lake stands a shrine to Kalijai. In one popular version of the tale, a newly married girl named Jai was crossing the lake by boat with her father to meet her husband's family on an island. A cyclone capsized the boat. The boatman and her father survived, but Jai was lost. The villagers came to see her as a goddess who protects people on the water, and the shrine still draws boatmen and pilgrims.
lesson: Respect the weather and pray for a safe crossing.

title: Narali Purnima, a Gift to the Sea
text: Every year after the monsoon, on the full-moon day of Shravan, Koli fishing families of Maharashtra gather on the shore. They offer a coconut to the sea to say thank you and to ask for safe journeys. The monsoon months are a rest time, when many fish breed. The coconut marks the day the boats go back to the water.
lesson: Give thanks, and let the sea rest so it can give again.

title: Rama's Bridge and the Little Squirrel
text: The Ramayana tells of the great bridge built across the sea to Lanka. Rama's army of vanaras dropped stones into the water, and the stones floated when Rama's name was written on them. A little squirrel also helped, rolling in the sand and shaking grains onto the bridge. Rama stroked her back in thanks. The chain of shoals between Rameswaram and Sri Lanka is known as Rama's Bridge, or Adam's Bridge.
lesson: Small help counts. Every hand matters.

title: Bombil used to come to the shore
text: When I was a boy the Bombil came so close in the monsoon that we could net them from the shore. Now the boats have to go much farther out to find them.

title: Chakara: when the sea turns muddy and calm
text: In the monsoon, in some places the sea near our beach turns muddy and calm. We call it chakara, and the fish, especially sardines, come in close. We watch the colour of the water to know.
summary_en: Calm, muddy water near the beach in the monsoon (chakara) brings fish, especially sardines, close to shore.

title: Reading the north-east wind
text: When the wind swings to the north-east and the clouds pile up over the sea at dusk, my father brought the boats in early. He read the sky, not a phone.

title: Clear water in Chilika
text: In Chilika the crabs and prawns are plentiful when the water is clear and the wind is light. We set the nets before sunrise.

title: Before we enter the creeks
text: Before we enter the creeks of the Sundarbans we call on Bonbibi. We go in groups, never alone, and we take only what we need.

title: Silver flashes at dawn
text: At first light we look for silver flashes on the water. That is the shoal. We circle it quietly with the net before the sun gets high.

title: The sea is taking our beach
text: The sea is taking the beach at our village. Our fathers' houses stood where the waves are now.

title: Follow the birds
text: We follow the birds. When they dive over one spot, the tuna are driving small fish to the surface. That is where we throw the bait.

title: Squid and the lamp
text: On calm nights we hang a bright lamp over the water. The squid come up to the light and we lift them in with small nets.

title: A strangely flat sea
text: When the sea goes strangely flat and quiet before the monsoon, we pull the boats high up the beach. The weather will turn soon.
